title: Thousands of servers can be backdoored by exploiting buggy motherboard controllers
why: Every enterprise server you run has a second always-on computer on its motherboard, and Black Hat research shows more than a dozen of those controllers, from HPE to Dell, can be remotely taken over to plant persistent backdoors that survive OS reinstalls and power-off.
notes: HD Moore of runZero disclosed more than a dozen new BMC vulnerabilities affecting hardware from HPE, Supermicro, Avocent, Huawei, Lenovo, and Dell; presentation was Wednesday at Black Hat in Las Vegas.

BMCs are embedded microcontrollers with their own OS firmware, network stack, and IP address, providing 'lights out' out-of-band management that keeps working when the host server is off or unresponsive.
Because BMCs can reboot machines, push updates, and reinstall the OS, code execution on one gives attackers deep, persistent access to the servers it manages.

The core IPMI protocol weaknesses were warned about as far back as 2013; Moore says some flaws he flagged then remain active despite measures meant to fix them, and some new bugs are more than a decade old.
Article reports the count ('more than a dozen') and affected vendors but does not include CVE identifiers, per-vulnerability technical detail, exploitation prerequisites, or patch status by vendor.
summary: At Black Hat 2026 in Las Vegas, firmware security researcher HD Moore, CEO of runZero, presented more than a dozen new vulnerabilities in baseboard management controllers (BMCs) sold by HPE, Supermicro, Avocent, Huawei, Lenovo, Dell, and others. BMCs are miniature computers embedded in nearly every enterprise server motherboard, running their own OS firmware, network stack, and IP address to provide out-of-band, 'lights out' management that functions even when the host is powered off. Moore's work argues that little has changed since researchers first warned in 2013 that BMCs and the IPMI protocol offer attackers a route to remote code execution and persistent datacenter access; some flaws he flagged then reportedly remain exploitable despite claimed fixes. Because a compromised BMC can reboot, update, and reinstall the OS of the server it manages, it functions as a durable backdoor. The article describes the vulnerability count and affected vendors but does not provide CVE identifiers, per-flaw technical detail, or vendor patch status.
novelty: new BMC vulns, decade-old flaws still unpatched
audience: datacenter/infra security teams, sysadmins managing server fleets

title: When AI Benchmarks Plateau: A Systematic Study of Benchmark Saturation
why: If you use benchmark scores to pick or ship models, this study says expert curation, not private test sets, is what keeps a benchmark discriminating; nearly half of the 60 benchmarks examined have already stopped separating models.
notes: Scope: 60 language-model benchmarks scored against 14 properties the authors define as related to saturation; the paper offers an explicit definition of what 'saturation' means rather than treating it informally.
Headline finding: nearly half the benchmarks studied exhibit saturation, and the saturation rate rises with a benchmark's age.

Mechanism claim: resilience to saturation tracks with expert curation of items, and is not explained by whether the test data is public or held out; this cuts against the common assumption that data contamination is the main driver.
Framing: benchmarks are treated as guiding deployment decisions, so saturation directly erodes their value for differentiating frontier models.

Caveats: this is an arXiv preprint (abstract only here); the list of which 60 benchmarks, the 14 properties, saturation thresholds, and how expert-curation was coded are not given in the provided text, so the causal claim can't be independently checked from the abstract.
summary: The paper defines benchmark saturation, the point at which a benchmark stops distinguishing between models, and studies it systematically across 60 language-model benchmarks using 14 saturation-related properties. It reports that nearly half the benchmarks show saturation and that the saturation rate increases with benchmark age. Its central mechanistic claim is that resistance to saturation correlates with expert curation of benchmark items, and not with whether the test data is public, suggesting contamination from public data is not the deciding factor. The authors conclude that specific design choices can extend a benchmark's useful lifespan and inform more durable evaluation methods. title: Pgtestdb's template cloning approach to testing is fast
why: Postgres template cloning bootstraps an isolated test database in ~100ms, roughly as fast as running migrations on a fresh schema, so the "creating databases is slow" assumption you've been designing test suites around is wrong.
notes: pgtestdb uses Postgres template databases (CREATE DATABASE dbname TEMPLATE template_to_copy); at the storage level Postgres copies the template's heap, index, and catalog files in 8kB page chunks, which is faster than migrating from scratch and far faster than Docker-based setups.

Per-test setup was near-identical: pgtestdb clone averaged 98.4ms (p90 247.4ms, p95 299.5ms, max 465.1ms) across 466 runs; River's create+migrate schema averaged 99.4ms (p90 152.1ms, p95 209.0ms, max 327.0ms) across 81 runs. These are the author's own measurements from splicing pgtestdb into River's suite via Codex.

Full suite wall time favored River's schema approach: 14.54s vs 51.07s for pgtestdb clone, about 3.5x faster. The edge is not faster creation but pooling: River reuses cleaned, unclaimed schemas across parallel tests instead of building each from scratch.
Postgres schemas are lighter-weight than databases but cannot be cloned, so the schema approach must re-run migrations each time; template cloning trades that off by copying a prebuilt database.
Reuse could be added to pgtestdb too; the author estimates pooling would cut bootstrap to 10-20ms, closer to test-transaction speed, which matters for suites approaching 10,000 tests.

Caveat: reuse requires tracking schema version so a test only reuses a schema at the version it expects; the author says River's pre-LLM implementation took a few days to debug. He is keeping River on schemas but will recommend pgtestdb in the docs for end-to-end testing.
summary: Brandur benchmarked Peter Downs' pgtestdb, a Go/Postgres testing package built on Postgres template databases (CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE), against River's existing schema-based test isolation. Cloning a template copies the source database's heap, index, and catalog files in 8kB pages, which is faster than migrating a fresh database and, in his tests, roughly as fast as creating and migrating a schema: 98.4ms mean for pgtestdb clone versus 99.4ms for schema create+migrate. Despite similar per-test setup, River's full suite ran ~3.5x faster (14.54s vs 51.07s) because River pools and reuses cleaned schemas across parallel test cases rather than creating each from scratch. Reuse requires care around schema versioning, and the same optimization could be applied to pgtestdb to drop bootstrap time to an estimated 10-20ms. The author will keep River on schemas but recommend pgtestdb in the docs for end-to-end testing. All numbers are the author's self-reported measurements from a single run against River's suite.
novelty: Benchmarked Postgres template-cloning vs schema-migration test isolation
audience: Backend engineers optimizing Go/Postgres test suite speed
